title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Operational Tooling, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This page defines Redwood Inference's company-wide standards for Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) documentation covering: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets; capacity planning and forecasting; reliability initiatives and roadmaps; incident review and postmortem standards; operational tooling (dashboards, alerts, tracing); and runbook structure and best practices. The intent is to ensure consistent, actionable guidance for owners, SREs, and on-call engineers so that reliability work is measurable, repeatable, and prioritized against product goals.

Scope

- Applies to all customer-facing and internal services that have production traffic (hosted API, control plane services, batch jobs, telemetry pipelines).
- Exclusions: short-lived prototypes, experimental feature flags that are explicitly labeled non-production.

Definitions

- SLI (Service Level Indicator): a measurable signal used to compute an SLO (e.g., request latency, success rate, queue depth).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): a target value for an SLI (e.g., 99.9% requests succeed within 300ms).
- Error budget: allowed amount of SLO violation within a rolling window (e.g., 0.1% downtime per 30 days).
- Burn rate: speed at which an error budget is being consumed compared to the baseline.

SLO and Error Budget Standards

1) Owner and SLI selection
   - Every service must have an SLO owner listed in the service README and in the SLO dashboard metadata.
   - Select 1-3 primary SLIs that map directly to customer impact: availability (success rate), latency (p95/p99), and correctness (error-free responses for critical routes).
   - SLIs must be instrumented in both production traces and the metric system (Prometheus / Cortex).

2) SLO targets and rolling windows
   - Default SLO tiers for customer-facing APIs (examples):
     | Tier | Availability SLO | Latency SLO (p95) | Window |
     |------|------------------|-------------------|--------|
     | Platinum | 99.99% | 150 ms | 30 days |
     | Gold     | 99.9%  | 300 ms | 30 days |
     | Silver   | 99.0%  | 500 ms | 30 days |
   - Internal infra and non-customer critical services may use relaxed targets but must document rationale.

3) Error budget policy and actions
   - Error budgets are evaluated on a rolling 30-day window by default. 7-day and 1-day burn-rate windows are used for alerting.
   - Alert thresholds (example):
     - Advisory: 30-day burn rate > 2x -> notify SLO owner (Slack + email).
     - Action required: 7-day burn rate > 4x -> pause feature rollouts, convene reliability working group.
     - Emergency: 1-day burn rate > 8x -> paging and immediate mitigation playbook.
   - When the error budget is exhausted, the SLO owner must:
     1) Open an "Error Budget Hold" ticket in the service backlog.
     2) Halt non-essential releases (feature flags may be rolled back).
     3) Prioritize reliability work until budget is partially restored.

Capacity Planning and Forecasting

- Goals: ensure headroom for predictable traffic patterns and burst resilience for peak events (model rollouts, customer demos, region failovers).
- Forecast cadence: weekly rolling forecasts for short-term capacity, and quarterly capacity planning for long-term purchases/reservations.
- Inputs for forecasts:
  1) Historical traffic (90/95/99 percentiles) and trend growth (last 90 days).
  2) Scheduled product events (model deployments, marketing campaigns).
  3) Business KPIs (expected customer growth, new large customers onboarding).
- Headroom policy: maintain >= 25% CPU/GPU headroom for regular traffic; during major model rollouts increase reserved capacity to meet expected token throughput.
- Burst policy: ensure autoscaling can add N additional nodes within T minutes: default N=25% of fleet, T=5 minutes for API services.

Capacity planning table (example)

| Service | Current Peak TPM | Required Headroom | Autoscale Target | Notes |
|---------|------------------:|------------------:|-----------------:|------|
| api-gateway | 12,000 | 30% | scale +3 nodes @ 75% cpu | Region eu-west-1 |
| model-serve-v2 | 1,200 tokens/s | 25% | scale +2 GPUs @ queue depth > 80 | Quantized models recommended |

Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

- Initiative types: corrective (post-incident fixes), preventive (load testing, chaos experiments), and detective (better SLIs, anomaly detection).
- Prioritization criteria: customer impact, probability, cost-to-fix, lift on MTTR or MTBF. Use standard RFC process and tag reliability-related PRs with label `reliability`.
- Quarterly reliability roadmap: teams must publish a 90-day plan with measurable goals (e.g., reduce p99 latency by 30% for /v1/generate; add caching to reduce token cost by 18%).

Incident Review and Postmortem Standards

- Post-incident timeline
  1) T+24h: acknowledge incident summary posted to incident channel.
  2) T+72h: draft postmortem created and assigned.
  3) T+7 days: final postmortem published with remediation plan and owners.
- Postmortem template (required fields):
  - Title, incident id, severity, start/end times (UTC), detection source, summary of impact, timeline of key events, root cause analysis, contributing factors, mitigation steps taken, follow-up actions (owner + due date), lessons learned, and metrics showing resolution.
- Blameless culture: focus on systemic fixes. Root causes should identify process, tooling, or capacity gaps rather than individuals.
- Severity classification (example):
  - Sev 1: customer-visible outage impacting >1% of traffic or critical SLAs.
  - Sev 2: partial degradation affecting a subset of customers or increased latencies.
  - Sev 3: minor issues with limited impact or internal-only services.

Operational Tooling Standards

- Dashboards: every service must publish an SLO dashboard that includes: SLI timeseries, error budget burn rate, recent deployments, and top 5 dependent services. Use the standard dashboard template (Grafana ID: infra-slo-template).
- Alerts: alert on symptoms (high error rate, queue growth) and on SLO burn (as defined above). Alerts should include runbook links, playbook steps, and escalation policies in the alert body.
- Tracing and logs: 100% of production requests must include trace IDs. Logs must be structured JSON with request_id, user_id (if available), trace_id, service, span, and error_code. Sensitive fields must be redacted at ingest.
- Synthetic testing: configure synthetics for critical user journeys with 1-minute cadence for API storefront routes and 5-minute cadence for model inference endpoints.

Runbook Standards and Examples

- Runbook structure (required sections):
  1) Runbook title and service owner.
  2) Symptom(s) that trigger this runbook.
  3) Priority and severity mapping.
  4) Quick triage checklist.
  5) Mitigation steps (short-term).
  6) Recovery steps (longer-term).
  7) Rollback / feature-flag instructions.
  8) Post-incident actions and links to postmortem template.
  9) Contact list and paging escalation matrix.

- Example: "High request error rate on /v1/generate" runbook (excerpt)
  - Symptom: p95 error rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes OR request success rate < 99% over 10 minutes.
  - Quick triage checklist:
    1) Check the SLO dashboard and recent deploys.
    2) Confirm whether deployments or config changes occurred in last 30 minutes.
    3) Determine whether a specific model shard/host is overloaded (see host-level metrics).
  - Mitigation steps:
    1) Roll back the most recent deployment if it correlates with increased errors.
    2) Scale up model-serving pool by +2 GPUs (automated script: ops/scale_gpus.sh --service model-serve-v2 --count 2).
    3) Enable degraded-mode routing: route traffic to a lower-latency model variant for 30 minutes (feature flag control).

Ownership, Reviews and Governance

- Ownership: every service must list an SLO owner and a backup on the service README and in the on-call rota. SLO owners are accountable for maintaining SLOs, dashboards, runbooks, and for driving error-budget remediation.
- Documentation reviews: SRE documentation (SLOs, runbooks, postmortem templates) must be reviewed at least every six months or after any Sev1 incident. Use the reviewers field in the page metadata to list reviewers.
- Audit: periodic checks by the SRE guild will validate that all production services have SLOs, dashboards, alerts, and runbooks. Findings published to the reliability dashboard.

How to use this page

- To add/update a service SLO: copy the SLO dashboard template, create the service dashboard, add the SLO owner, and create a short SLO definition page linking to this standards doc.
- To create a new runbook: follow the runbook template and ensure it is linked from the service README and in alerts.

References and templates

- SLO dashboard template: Grafana ID infra-slo-template (link internal).
- Postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template-2025.
- Runbook template: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template-2025.
